decks.title: Breathing and Exchange of Gases — Part 1: Respiratory organs and the mechanism of breathing
goals: Relate the respiratory organs of different animals to their habitat and level of organisation
Describe the human respiratory system and the conducting and exchange parts
Explain inspiration and expiration in terms of muscles, volume and pressure
Define the respiratory volumes and capacities and calculate one from the others

slides.heading: Breathing and Exchange of Gases
slides.body_md: Part 1 — where animals take in oxygen, the human respiratory system, and how air is moved in and out of the lungs.

visual.alt: Flow of the five steps of respiration from breathing to the use of oxygen by cells

slides.narration: Cells need oxygen to break down nutrients such as glucose for energy, and they release carbon dioxide, which is harmful and must be removed. Taking in atmospheric oxygen and giving out the carbon dioxide made by cells is called breathing, or more commonly, respiration.

slides.heading: Respiratory organs in animals
slides.body_md: The mechanism of breathing varies with the **habitat** and the **level of organisation** of the animal.

rows: Simple diffusion over the whole body surface
Network of tracheal tubes carrying air into the body
Most aquatic arthropods and molluscs; fishes
Terrestrial forms: amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals
Lungs (pulmonary respiration); frogs also through moist skin (cutaneous respiration)

visual.alt: Table of animal groups and their respiratory surfaces or organs

slides.narration: Small and simple animals exchange gases over the whole body surface. An earthworm uses its moist cuticle and an insect sends air through tracheal tubes. Aquatic animals mostly use gills, while land vertebrates use lungs. A frog can also exchange gases through its moist skin.

slides.heading: The human respiratory system
slides.body_md: Air passes from the **external nostrils** through the **nasal passage** and **nasal chamber** into the **pharynx**, a common passage for food and air, then through the **larynx** into the **trachea**. The trachea divides at the level of the **fifth thoracic vertebra** into the right and left **primary bronchi**, which branch into secondary and tertiary bronchi and **bronchioles**, ending in **alveoli**.

slides.narration: The larynx is a cartilaginous box that helps in sound production, so it is called the sound box. During swallowing the glottis is covered by the epiglottis, a thin elastic flap of cartilage, so that food does not enter the larynx. The trachea, the bronchi and the first bronchioles are held open by incomplete rings of cartilage.

slides.heading: Conducting part and exchange part
slides.body_md: Each terminal bronchiole gives rise to many very thin, irregular-walled, vascularised bag-like **alveoli**. The branching network of bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli makes up the **lungs**.

rows: External nostrils up to the terminal bronchioles
Transports air to the alveoli, clears it of foreign particles, humidifies it and brings it to body temperature
Actual diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide between blood and air

visual.alt: Table comparing the conducting and exchange parts of the respiratory system

slides.narration: Most of the airway only conducts air. On the way it is cleaned, moistened and warmed or cooled to body temperature. Gases are exchanged with blood only in the alveoli and their ducts, the exchange part.

slides.heading: The thoracic chamber and the pleura
slides.body_md: The lungs lie in the **thoracic chamber**, which is **anatomically air-tight**. Any change in its volume is reflected in the lung (pulmonary) cavity; we cannot directly alter the pulmonary volume.

rows: Double-layered pleura with pleural fluid between the layers, which reduces friction on the lung surface

visual.alt: Table of the boundaries of the thoracic chamber and the covering of the lungs

slides.narration: The outer pleural membrane is in close contact with the lining of the thoracic chamber and the inner one with the lung surface. Because the chamber is sealed, changing its size changes the size of the lungs, and this is how we breathe.

slides.heading: Five steps of respiration
slides.body_md: Respiration involves the following steps.

nodes.label: Breathing (pulmonary ventilation): atmospheric air in, carbon dioxide-rich alveolar air out
Diffusion of gases across the alveolar membrane
Transport of gases by the blood
Diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide between blood and tissues
Utilisation of oxygen by cells for catabolic reactions and release of carbon dioxide (cellular respiration)

visual.alt: Flow of the five steps of respiration

slides.narration: Breathing only moves air. Gases then diffuse across the alveolar membrane, travel in the blood, diffuse again between blood and tissues, and finally oxygen is used by cells in cellular respiration, which is studied in another chapter.

slides.heading: Mechanism of breathing
slides.body_md: Breathing has two stages: **inspiration**, when air is drawn in, and **expiration**, when alveolar air is released. Air moves because of a **pressure gradient** between the lungs and the atmosphere, created with the help of the **diaphragm** and the **external and internal intercostal muscles** between the ribs.

slides.narration: Inspiration happens when the pressure inside the lungs, the intra-pulmonary pressure, is less than atmospheric pressure, that is, when there is a negative pressure in the lungs. Expiration happens when the intra-pulmonary pressure is higher than atmospheric pressure.

slides.heading: Inspiration and expiration compared
slides.body_md: Increasing the thoracic volume increases the pulmonary volume, which lowers the intra-pulmonary pressure.

rows: Contracts: volume rises in the antero-posterior axis
Relaxes and returns to its dome shape
Contract: lift ribs and sternum, volume rises in the dorso-ventral axis

visual.alt: Table comparing inspiration and expiration

slides.narration: With the help of extra muscles in the abdomen we can make inspiration and expiration stronger. A healthy person at rest breathes twelve to sixteen times a minute.

slides.heading: Respiratory volumes and capacities
slides.body_md: The volume of air in breathing movements is estimated with a **spirometer**. Typical adult values (mL): tidal volume about **500**; inspiratory reserve volume **2500–3000**; expiratory reserve volume **1000–1100**; residual volume **1100–1200**. The spirogram is drawn with the upper values.

slides.narration: Tidal volume is the air moved in or out in one normal breath, about five hundred millilitres. Reserve volumes are the extra air we can forcibly breathe in or out. Residual volume stays in the lungs even after the most forcible expiration.

slides.heading: Capacities are sums of volumes
slides.body_md: With the lower values (500, 2500, 1000, 1100 mL for TV, IRV, ERV, RV) and the upper values (500, 3000, 1100, 1200 mL) the capacities are:

rows: RV + ERV + TV + IRV, or VC + RV

visual.alt: Table of the five capacities with their sums and values

slides.narration: Vital capacity is the most air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration, or breathe out after a forced inspiration. Total lung capacity is all the air in the lungs at the end of a forced inspiration, which is vital capacity plus residual volume.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: capacities from readings
slides.body_md: A student’s readings (mL) are TV 500, IRV 2800, ERV 1050, and RV 1150 (estimated, as a spirometer cannot measure it). Find her VC, TLC and FRC.
bullets: $\text{VC} = \text{ERV} + \text{TV} + \text{IRV} = 1050 + 500 + 2800 = 4350$ mL.
$\text{TLC} = \text{VC} + \text{RV} = 4350 + 1150 = 5500$ mL.
$\text{FRC} = \text{ERV} + \text{RV} = 1050 + 1150 = 2200$ mL.

visual.alt: Worked table: VC 4350, TLC 5500, FRC 2200 mL

slides.narration: Always write the sum first, then put in the numbers. Vital capacity adds the three volumes that can be breathed out. Total lung capacity adds the residual volume as well. Functional residual capacity is the air left after a normal breath out.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: air breathed in a minute
slides.body_md: A person at rest has a tidal volume of 500 mL and breathes 14 times a minute. While climbing stairs the rate rises to 20 a minute with the same tidal volume. How much air is moved in a minute in each case?
bullets: At rest: $500 \times 14 = 7000$ mL per minute.
Climbing: $500 \times 20 = 10000$ mL per minute.
A healthy person can inspire or expire about 6000 to 8000 mL of air per minute at rest.

visual.alt: Worked table: 7000 and 10000 mL of air per minute

slides.narration: Multiply the tidal volume by the number of breaths in a minute. At rest this person moves seven thousand millilitres a minute, inside the usual range of six to eight thousand. Faster breathing moves ten thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: capacities
slides.body_md: Which two volumes add up to the functional residual capacity?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is the air left in the lungs after a normal expiration.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Respiratory surfaces: body surface, moist cuticle, tracheal tubes, gills, lungs; frogs also use moist skin.
Nostrils → nasal chamber → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli; epiglottis guards the glottis.
Conducting part cleans, humidifies and warms air; alveoli are the exchange part.
Thoracic chamber is air-tight; lungs covered by a double pleura with pleural fluid.
Inspiration: diaphragm and external intercostals contract, volume up, pressure below atmospheric.
Volumes: TV about 500, IRV 2500–3000, ERV 1000–1100, RV 1100–1200 mL; capacities are their sums.

visual.alt: Summary table of the two stages of breathing

slides.narration: To recap: different animals use different respiratory surfaces. In humans, air is conducted to the alveoli, where exchange happens. We breathe by changing the volume of an air-tight chest. And the respiratory capacities are simply sums of the four respiratory volumes.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Draw the **respiratory system** with at least eight labels, including the **epiglottis** and **pleura**.
Name the **axis** each muscle changes: diaphragm antero-posterior, external intercostals dorso-ventral.
Write each **capacity as a sum** before putting in numbers; give units (mL).
Remember a spirometer **cannot** measure residual volume.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Practise a labelled diagram of the respiratory system. Link the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles to the axis they change. Write each capacity as a sum before calculating. And remember that residual volume cannot be breathed out, so a spirometer cannot measure it.

slides.narration: Alveoli are the primary sites of exchange of gases, and gases are also exchanged between blood and tissues. Both exchanges happen by simple diffusion, driven by differences in pressure or concentration.

slides.narration: The pressure that one gas contributes in a mixture is its partial pressure. Oxygen moves from alveolar air, where its partial pressure is high, into the blood, where it is low. Carbon dioxide moves the other way, from the blood into the alveoli.

slides.heading: Partial pressures (mm Hg)
slides.body_md: Solubility of the gases and the thickness of the membranes also affect the rate of diffusion.

visual.alt: Table of the partial pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide at five sites

slides.narration: Read the table along each row. Oxygen falls from the alveoli to the tissues, so it diffuses from alveoli to blood and from blood to tissues. Carbon dioxide is highest in the tissues, so it diffuses from tissues to blood and from blood to the alveoli.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: comparing the gradients
slides.body_md: From the table, find the partial-pressure difference for each gas between alveolar air and the deoxygenated blood reaching the lungs. Why is carbon dioxide still exchanged well?
bullets: Oxygen: $104 - 40 = 64$ mm Hg, from alveoli to blood.
Carbon dioxide: $45 - 40 = 5$ mm Hg, from blood to alveoli.
The solubility of carbon dioxide is **20–25 times** that of oxygen, so much more carbon dioxide diffuses for each unit of pressure difference.

visual.alt: Worked table: oxygen gradient 64, carbon dioxide gradient 5 mm Hg

slides.narration: The oxygen gradient is sixty-four, the carbon dioxide gradient only five. Even so, carbon dioxide is twenty to twenty-five times more soluble than oxygen, so it crosses the membrane readily. All the factors in our body favour oxygen moving from alveoli to tissues and carbon dioxide moving the opposite way.

slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the diffusion of the two gases.

slides.heading: Transport of oxygen
slides.body_md: Blood carries about **97 percent** of oxygen in the **red blood cells** and the remaining **3 percent** dissolved in the **plasma**. **Haemoglobin**, a red iron-containing pigment, binds oxygen reversibly to form **oxyhaemoglobin**; each haemoglobin molecule can carry at most **four** molecules of oxygen.

rows: High pO₂, low pCO₂, fewer H⁺ ions, lower temperature (alveoli)
Low pO₂, high pCO₂, more H⁺ ions, higher temperature (tissues)

slides.narration: Binding of oxygen to haemoglobin depends mainly on the partial pressure of oxygen. The partial pressure of carbon dioxide, hydrogen ion concentration and temperature can also interfere with this binding.

slides.body_md: A plot of the **percentage saturation of haemoglobin** with oxygen against **pO₂** is a **sigmoid** curve, the **oxygen dissociation curve**. It shows how factors such as pCO₂ and H⁺ concentration affect binding.

slides.narration: In the alveoli, haemoglobin is almost fully loaded with oxygen. In the tissues, where the partial pressure of oxygen is low and carbon dioxide, acidity and temperature are higher, oxygen dissociates and is released. The values on the curve come from a standard model and are only illustrative.

slides.heading: Quick check: oxygen in plasma
slides.body_md: What share of the oxygen carried by blood is dissolved in the plasma?
slides.narration: Quick check. Almost all oxygen travels with haemoglobin. How much is left for the plasma?

slides.heading: Transport of carbon dioxide
slides.body_md: About **20–25 percent** of carbon dioxide travels as **carbamino-haemoglobin**, about **70 percent** as **bicarbonate** and about **7 percent** dissolved in plasma. The enzyme **carbonic anhydrase**, present at high concentration in RBCs and in minute quantities in plasma, speeds up the reaction both ways.

visual.alt: Carbon dioxide and water form carbonic acid, which forms bicarbonate and hydrogen ions, catalysed by carbonic anhydrase
visual.caption: Carbonic anhydrase speeds both directions

math: \ce{CO2 + H2O <=>[\text{carbonic anhydrase}] H2CO3 <=>[\text{carbonic anhydrase}] HCO3- + H+}
slides.narration: In the tissues, where carbon dioxide is high, the reaction runs forward and bicarbonate forms. In the alveoli, where carbon dioxide is low, it runs backward and carbon dioxide is released. High carbon dioxide and low oxygen favour carbamino-haemoglobin in tissues; the opposite conditions in the alveoli release the carbon dioxide.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: oxygen delivered to the tissues
slides.body_md: Under normal conditions every 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL of oxygen to the tissues, and every 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of carbon dioxide to the alveoli. How much of each gas is exchanged when 5000 mL of blood passes?
bullets: Oxygen: $\dfrac{5000}{100} \times 5 = 250$ mL.
Carbon dioxide: $\dfrac{5000}{100} \times 4 = 200$ mL.
Only part of the oxygen carried is unloaded at rest; the rest is a reserve.

visual.alt: Worked table: 250 mL oxygen and 200 mL carbon dioxide

slides.narration: Divide the blood volume by one hundred to find how many hundred-millilitre portions there are, then multiply by the amount each portion delivers. Five thousand millilitres of blood unloads about two hundred and fifty millilitres of oxygen and gives up about two hundred millilitres of carbon dioxide.

slides.heading: Regulation of respiration
slides.body_md: Humans can adjust the rhythm of breathing to the demands of the body tissues; this is done by the **neural system**.

nodes.label: Chemosensitive area beside the rhythm centre senses more CO₂ and H⁺
Receptors at the aortic arch and carotid artery also sense CO₂ and H⁺
Pneumotaxic centre (pons): can shorten inspiration and alter rate
Breathing muscles adjust rate and depth

visual.alt: Flow of the regulation of breathing by the medulla, the pons and chemical sensors

slides.narration: The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla is primarily responsible for regulation. The pneumotaxic centre in the pons can moderate it, reducing the duration of inspiration and thereby altering the rate. A rise in carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions activates the chemosensitive area. The role of oxygen in regulating the rhythm is quite insignificant.

slides.heading: Quick check: rhythm centre
slides.body_md: Where is the respiratory rhythm centre located?
slides.narration: Quick check. It lies in the hindbrain, close to the spinal cord.

slides.heading: Disorders of the respiratory system
slides.body_md: Three disorders named in the syllabus.

rows: Difficulty in breathing with wheezing, due to inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles
Often triggered by irritants such as pollen or dust
A chronic disorder in which the alveolar walls are damaged, so the respiratory surface decreases
Cigarette smoking is one of the major causes
Long exposure to dust causes inflammation and fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissue), with serious lung damage
Stone-grinding or stone-breaking industries; prevented by protective masks

visual.alt: Table of asthma, emphysema and occupational respiratory disorders

slides.narration: In some industries, especially stone grinding or breaking, so much dust is produced that the body’s defences cannot cope. Workers in such places should wear protective masks.

slides.body_md: Which disorder is described: alveolar walls are damaged and the respiratory surface is reduced?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which chronic disorder is linked with smoking?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Exchange by simple diffusion; diffusion membrane of three layers, much less than a millimetre thick.
pO₂: alveoli 104, tissues 40; pCO₂: alveoli 40, tissues 45 mm Hg; CO₂ is 20–25 times more soluble.
Oxygen: 97 percent as oxyhaemoglobin, 3 percent in plasma; sigmoid dissociation curve.
Carbon dioxide: 20–25 percent carbamino-haemoglobin, 70 percent bicarbonate, 7 percent dissolved; carbonic anhydrase.
Regulation: rhythm centre (medulla), pneumotaxic centre (pons), chemosensitive area; oxygen plays little part.
Disorders: asthma, emphysema, occupational disorders (fibrosis; use masks).

visual.alt: Summary table of the main transport form of each gas

slides.narration: To recap: gases move by diffusion down their partial pressure gradients. Haemoglobin carries most of the oxygen, and most carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate. The brain sets the rhythm of breathing, mainly in response to carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions.

State the **three layers** of the diffusion membrane.
Give the **percentages** for oxygen and carbon dioxide transport and the role of **carbonic anhydrase**.
Name **where** each centre lies: rhythm centre in the medulla, pneumotaxic centre in the pons.

sections.heading: 1. Respiratory organs and the human respiratory system
sections.body_md:
Organisms use oxygen to break down simple molecules such as glucose, amino acids and fatty acids for energy, and this releases harmful **carbon dioxide**. Exchange of atmospheric oxygen with the carbon dioxide produced by cells is called **breathing**, commonly known as respiration.

**Respiratory organs** vary with habitat and level of organisation:
- **Sponges, coelenterates and flatworms:** simple diffusion over the entire body surface.
- **Earthworms:** moist cuticle. **Insects:** a network of tubes (**tracheal tubes**) carrying atmospheric air within the body.
- **Most aquatic arthropods and molluscs:** special vascularised structures, **gills** (branchial respiration). **Terrestrial forms:** vascularised bags, **lungs** (pulmonary respiration).
- **Vertebrates:** fishes use gills; reptiles, birds and mammals respire through lungs; **amphibians** such as frogs use lungs and can also respire through their **moist skin** (cutaneous respiration).

**Human respiratory system.** A pair of **external nostrils** opens out above the upper lip and leads through the **nasal passage** to the **nasal chamber**, which opens into the **pharynx**, a common passage for food and air. The pharynx opens through the **larynx** into the **trachea**. The larynx is a cartilaginous box that helps in sound production and is called the **sound box**. During swallowing the glottis is covered by the **epiglottis**, a thin elastic cartilaginous flap, to prevent the entry of food into the larynx.

The **trachea** is a straight tube extending up to the mid-thoracic cavity, where it divides at the level of the **fifth thoracic vertebra** into right and left **primary bronchi**. Each bronchus undergoes repeated divisions into secondary and tertiary bronchi and **bronchioles**, ending in very thin **terminal bronchioles**. The tracheae, primary, secondary and tertiary bronchi and initial bronchioles are supported by **incomplete cartilaginous rings**. Each terminal bronchiole gives rise to many very thin, irregular-walled, vascularised bag-like structures called **alveoli**. The branching network of bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli makes up the **lungs**.

The two lungs are covered by a **double-layered pleura**, with **pleural fluid** between the layers that **reduces friction** on the lung surface. The outer pleural membrane is in close contact with the thoracic lining and the inner one with the lung surface.

- **Conducting part:** from the external nostrils up to the terminal bronchioles; transports air to the alveoli, clears it of foreign particles, **humidifies** it and brings it to **body temperature**.
- **Exchange (respiratory) part:** the **alveoli and their ducts**, the sites of actual diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide between blood and air.

The lungs lie in the **thoracic chamber**, which is **anatomically air-tight**: it is formed dorsally by the **vertebral column**, ventrally by the **sternum**, laterally by the **ribs** and on the lower side by the dome-shaped **diaphragm**. Any change in its volume is reflected in the lung (pulmonary) cavity, which is essential for breathing because we cannot directly alter the pulmonary volume.

**Steps of respiration:** (i) breathing or pulmonary ventilation; (ii) diffusion of gases (oxygen and carbon dioxide) across the alveolar membrane; (iii) transport of gases by the blood; (iv) diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide between blood and tissues; (v) utilisation of oxygen by the cells for catabolic reactions and the resultant release of carbon dioxide (cellular respiration).

sections.heading: 2. Mechanism of breathing and respiratory volumes
sections.body_md:
Breathing involves **inspiration**, during which atmospheric air is drawn in, and **expiration**, by which alveolar air is released. Air moves because a **pressure gradient** is created between the lungs and the atmosphere. **Inspiration** occurs when the pressure within the lungs (**intra-pulmonary pressure**) is **less than atmospheric pressure**, that is, when there is a negative pressure in the lungs with respect to the atmosphere. **Expiration** occurs when the intra-pulmonary pressure is **higher than atmospheric pressure**.

The **diaphragm** and a specialised set of muscles, the **external and internal intercostals** between the ribs, help to generate these gradients.
- **Inspiration:** the **diaphragm contracts**, increasing the volume of the thoracic chamber in the **antero-posterior axis**; the **external intercostal muscles contract**, lifting the ribs and the sternum and increasing the volume in the **dorso-ventral axis**. The increase in thoracic volume causes a similar increase in pulmonary volume, the intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, and air moves into the lungs.
- **Expiration:** the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles **relax**, returning the diaphragm and sternum to their normal positions; the thoracic and pulmonary volumes decrease, the intra-pulmonary pressure rises slightly above atmospheric pressure, and air is expelled.
- Additional muscles in the **abdomen** can increase the strength of inspiration and expiration.

A healthy human breathes **12–16 times a minute**. The volume of air involved in breathing movements can be estimated with a **spirometer**, which helps in the clinical assessment of pulmonary functions.

**Respiratory volumes** (typical adult values; individual values vary with age, sex, size and fitness):
- **Tidal volume (TV):** volume of air inspired or expired during a normal respiration, about **500 mL**; a healthy person can inspire or expire about **6000 to 8000 mL of air per minute**.
- **Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV):** additional volume a person can inspire by a forcible inspiration, about **2500–3000 mL**.
- **Expiratory reserve volume (ERV):** additional volume a person can expire by a forcible expiration, about **1000–1100 mL**.
- **Residual volume (RV):** volume of air remaining in the lungs even after a forcible expiration, about **1100–1200 mL**.

**Respiratory capacities** are sums of volumes (values with the lower and upper ends of the ranges):
- **Inspiratory capacity (IC)** = TV + IRV: total air a person can inspire after a normal expiration (3000–3500 mL).
- **Expiratory capacity (EC)** = TV + ERV: total air a person can expire after a normal inspiration (1500–1600 mL).
- **Functional residual capacity (FRC)** = ERV + RV: air that remains in the lungs after a normal expiration (2100–2300 mL).
- **Vital capacity (VC)** = ERV + TV + IRV: the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration, or breathe out after a forced inspiration (4000–4600 mL).
- **Total lung capacity (TLC)** = RV + ERV + TV + IRV, or VC + RV: total air in the lungs at the end of a forced inspiration (5100–5800 mL).

The lower set uses TV 500, IRV 2500, ERV 1000, RV 1100 mL; the upper set uses TV 500, IRV 3000, ERV 1100, RV 1200 mL. Because residual volume never leaves the lungs, a spirometer cannot measure RV, FRC or TLC directly.

sections.heading: 3. Exchange and transport of gases; regulation of respiration
sections.body_md:
**Exchange of gases.** The **alveoli** are the primary sites of exchange of gases; exchange also occurs between blood and tissues. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged at these sites by **simple diffusion**, mainly based on pressure or concentration gradients. The **solubility** of the gases and the **thickness of the membranes** involved are also important.

The pressure contributed by an individual gas in a mixture is its **partial pressure**, written pO₂ for oxygen and pCO₂ for carbon dioxide.

| Gas | Atmospheric air | Alveoli | Deoxygenated blood | Oxygenated blood | Tissues |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| O₂ (mm Hg) | 159 | 104 | 40 | 95 | 40 |
| CO₂ (mm Hg) | 0.3 | 40 | 45 | 40 | 45 |

The data show a concentration gradient for oxygen from alveoli to blood and from blood to tissues, and the opposite gradient for carbon dioxide, from tissues to blood and from blood to alveoli. The solubility of carbon dioxide is **20–25 times higher** than that of oxygen, so the amount of carbon dioxide that can diffuse through the diffusion membrane per unit difference in partial pressure is much higher than that of oxygen.

The **diffusion membrane** has three major layers: the thin **squamous epithelium of the alveoli**, the **endothelium of the alveolar capillaries** and the **basement substance** in between; its total thickness is **much less than a millimetre**. All the factors in our body are therefore favourable for diffusion of oxygen from alveoli to tissues and of carbon dioxide from tissues to alveoli.

**Transport of oxygen.** About **97 percent** of oxygen is transported by the **RBCs** and the remaining **3 percent** is carried in a dissolved state in the **plasma**. **Haemoglobin** is a red-coloured, iron-containing pigment in the RBCs. Oxygen binds with haemoglobin reversibly to form **oxyhaemoglobin**; each haemoglobin molecule can carry a maximum of **four** molecules of oxygen. Binding depends primarily on **pO₂**; **pCO₂**, **hydrogen ion concentration** and **temperature** also interfere. A plot of the percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen against pO₂ gives a **sigmoid** curve, the **oxygen dissociation curve**. In the **alveoli**, high pO₂, low pCO₂, fewer H⁺ ions and lower temperature favour the **formation of oxyhaemoglobin**; in the **tissues**, low pO₂, high pCO₂, more H⁺ ions and higher temperature favour **dissociation** of oxygen. Every **100 mL** of oxygenated blood can deliver around **5 mL of oxygen** to the tissues under normal physiological conditions. (The saturation values printed on the curve, about 97 and 75 percent, come from a standard model and are illustrative.)

**Transport of carbon dioxide.** About **20–25 percent** of carbon dioxide is carried by haemoglobin as **carbamino-haemoglobin**, about **70 percent** as **bicarbonate**, and about **7 percent** dissolved in plasma. Binding is related to pCO₂; pO₂ is a major factor that affects it. In the tissues, where pCO₂ is high and pO₂ low, more carbon dioxide binds; in the alveoli, where pCO₂ is low and pO₂ high, carbon dioxide dissociates from carbamino-haemoglobin. RBCs contain a very high concentration of the enzyme **carbonic anhydrase** (minute quantities are present in plasma), which catalyses the reaction in both directions:

$$\ce{CO2 + H2O <=> H2CO3 <=> HCO3- + H+}$$

At the tissues carbon dioxide is trapped as bicarbonate; at the alveoli the reaction runs the opposite way and carbon dioxide is released. Every **100 mL** of deoxygenated blood delivers approximately **4 mL of carbon dioxide** to the alveoli.

**Regulation of respiration.** Humans can moderate the respiratory rhythm to suit the demands of the body tissues; this is done by the **neural system**.
- A specialised centre in the **medulla**, the **respiratory rhythm centre**, is primarily responsible for this regulation.
- The **pneumotaxic centre** in the **pons** can moderate the functions of the rhythm centre; its neural signal can reduce the duration of inspiration and thereby alter the respiratory rate.
- A **chemosensitive area** situated adjacent to the rhythm centre is highly sensitive to **carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions**; an increase in these activates it, and it signals the rhythm centre to make adjustments so that these substances are eliminated.
- **Receptors associated with the aortic arch and carotid artery** can also recognise changes in carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion concentration and send signals to the rhythm centre.
- The role of **oxygen** in the regulation of respiratory rhythm is **quite insignificant**.

sections.heading: 4. Disorders of the respiratory system
sections.body_md:
- **Asthma:** difficulty in breathing causing **wheezing**, due to **inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles**.
- **Emphysema:** a **chronic** disorder in which the **alveolar walls are damaged**, due to which the **respiratory surface is decreased**. One of the major causes is **cigarette smoking**.
- **Occupational respiratory disorders:** in certain industries, especially those involving **grinding or stone-breaking**, so much dust is produced that the defence mechanism of the body cannot fully cope with it. Long exposure can give rise to **inflammation** leading to **fibrosis** (proliferation of fibrous tissues) and thus cause serious lung damage. Workers in such industries should wear **protective masks**.

The conducting part normally traps and clears foreign particles; these disorders appear when irritants inflame the airways, when the alveolar surface is destroyed, or when dust exposure overwhelms the body’s defences.

key_terms.definition_md: Difficulty in breathing with wheezing, caused by inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles.
Chronic disorder in which alveolar walls are damaged and the respiratory surface decreases; smoking is a major cause.
Proliferation of fibrous tissue, here in the lungs after long exposure to dust.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying the diaphragm **relaxes** during inspiration (it contracts and flattens).
- Mixing up the axes: diaphragm changes the **antero-posterior** axis, external intercostals the **dorso-ventral** axis.
- Calling vital capacity the total air in the lungs (that is total lung capacity; VC excludes residual volume).
- Claiming a spirometer measures residual volume.
- Writing that most carbon dioxide travels as carbamino-haemoglobin (most travels as **bicarbonate**, about 70 percent).
- Placing the pneumotaxic centre in the medulla (it is in the **pons**).
- Saying a low oxygen level is the main stimulus for breathing (carbon dioxide and H⁺ are; oxygen’s role is insignificant).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: name a structure, a volume, a percentage, a centre or a disorder; assertion-reason on mechanism or transport.
- 2–3-mark answers: steps of respiration; conducting and exchange parts; capacities as sums; transport of carbon dioxide with the equation; asthma vs emphysema.
- 5-mark answers: the respiratory system with a diagram; the mechanism of breathing; exchange and transport of gases; regulation.
- Case-based items: spirometer readings, partial-pressure tables, exercise and breathing, dust exposure at work, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: A grasshopper’s blood carries very little oxygen, yet its flight muscles receive plenty while it jumps and flies. Which feature of its respiratory system explains this?

options.text_md: A pair of lungs opening at the mouth
Feathery gills folded under the abdomen
A moist cuticle richly supplied with blood vessels
A network of tracheal tubes that carries air directly into the body

questions.solution_md: Insects have a network of tubes (tracheal tubes) that carry atmospheric air within the body, so the blood need not transport oxygen — option (d).

questions.stem_md: After a heavy shower, an earthworm crawls onto a sunny concrete path and dies within an hour as its body surface dries. How is this linked to the way it exchanges gases?

options.text_md: It respires through its moist cuticle, which cannot exchange gases once dry.
Its gills collapse when they are out of water.
Its lungs fill with dust from the dry path.
Its tracheal tubes close in strong sunlight.

questions.solution_md: Earthworms use their moist cuticle for exchange of gases; a dry cuticle stops diffusion — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A frog spends the cold months buried in damp mud, hardly using its lungs at all. Which respiratory surface keeps it alive?
questions.solution_md: Amphibians such as frogs can respire through their moist skin — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which structure covers the glottis during swallowing so that food does not enter the larynx?
questions.solution_md: The epiglottis, a thin elastic cartilaginous flap, covers the glottis during swallowing — option (a).

questions.stem_md: At the level of which vertebra does the human trachea divide into the right and left primary bronchi?
questions.solution_md: The trachea extends up to the mid-thoracic cavity and divides at the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra — option (c).

questions.stem_md: After throat surgery, a patient breathes for some days through a tube placed directly in the trachea, so inhaled air bypasses the nose. Which normal function of the conducting part is she most likely to lose?

options.text_md: Exchange of oxygen with the blood in the alveoli
Binding of oxygen to haemoglobin in red blood cells
Humidifying the air and bringing it to body temperature
Contraction of the diaphragm during inspiration

questions.solution_md: The conducting part from the nostrils clears, humidifies and warms the air; gas exchange, oxygen binding and the diaphragm are not functions of the bypassed airway — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The figure shows the human respiratory system with five parts marked A to E. Which letter marks the straight tube that is held open by incomplete cartilaginous rings and divides at the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra?
questions.solution_md: A is the epiglottis, B the larynx, C the trachea, D a primary bronchus and E the diaphragm. The trachea, supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings, divides into the two primary bronchi — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Each human lung is covered by a double-layered pleura with fluid between the two layers.

**Reason (R):** The pleural fluid reduces friction on the lung surface.

Choose the correct option.

A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and reducing friction as the lungs move is the role of the fluid-filled double pleura — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A museum display groups four animals by the way they exchange gases. Match each animal (column I) with its main respiratory surface or organ (column II).
questions.solution_md: Earthworm: moist cuticle; cockroach (an insect): tracheal tubes; fish: gills; bird: lungs.

questions.stem_md: The floor of the air-tight thoracic chamber is formed by the dome-shaped ______.
questions.solution_md: The diaphragm forms the lower side of the thoracic chamber.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The larynx is a cartilaginous box that helps in sound production and is therefore called the sound box.
questions.solution_md: True.

questions.stem_md: A child inhales a speck of chalk dust in class. Name, in order, the parts it would pass if it travelled from the external nostrils all the way to an alveolus, and say which part of the system normally stops such particles.

answer.model_answer_md: External nostrils → **nasal passage** → **nasal chamber** → **pharynx** → **larynx** (through the glottis) → **trachea** → **primary bronchus** → secondary and tertiary bronchi → **bronchioles** → **terminal bronchiole** → **alveolus**. Normally the **conducting part** (nostrils to terminal bronchioles) **clears inhaled air of foreign particles**, so the dust would usually be trapped long before reaching the alveoli.

questions.solution_md: Correct sequence and role of the conducting part.

questions.stem_md: List, in the correct order, the five steps involved in respiration, from breathing to the use of oxygen by cells.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Breathing (pulmonary ventilation):** atmospheric air is drawn in and carbon dioxide-rich alveolar air is released.
2. **Diffusion** of oxygen and carbon dioxide across the **alveolar membrane**.
3. **Transport** of the gases by the **blood**.
4. **Diffusion** of oxygen and carbon dioxide between **blood and tissues**.
5. **Utilisation of oxygen by cells** for catabolic reactions and release of carbon dioxide (**cellular respiration**).

questions.solution_md: Five steps in order.

questions.stem_md: A knife wound lets outside air into the space between the two pleural layers on one side of the chest. Explain why the lung on that side stops filling with air even though the chest still moves.

answer.model_answer_md: Breathing works only because the **thoracic chamber is air-tight**, so a rise in thoracic volume is passed to the lung and **lowers the intra-pulmonary pressure**. With air in the pleural space the seal is broken: the chest expands but the **lung does not expand**, its pressure does not fall below atmospheric, and **no air is drawn in**.

questions.solution_md: Air-tight chamber needed for the pressure fall.

marking_scheme.step: Air-tight chamber passes volume change to lung
Seal broken: no pressure fall, no inspiration

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the conducting part and the exchange part of the human respiratory system, giving the extent and function of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Conducting part:** from the **external nostrils up to the terminal bronchioles**; it transports air to the alveoli, **clears** it of foreign particles, **humidifies** it and brings it to **body temperature**.

**Exchange (respiratory) part:** the **alveoli and their ducts**, where oxygen and carbon dioxide actually **diffuse** between blood and air.

questions.solution_md: Extent and function of each part.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of the human respiratory system from the external nostrils to the alveoli, including the thoracic chamber in which the lungs lie. Draw a labelled diagram.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Upper passages.** A pair of external nostrils opens above the upper lip and leads through the nasal passage into the nasal chamber, which opens into the pharynx, a common passage for food and air. The pharynx opens through the larynx into the trachea. The larynx is a cartilaginous box that helps in sound production (the sound box). During swallowing the glottis is covered by the epiglottis, a thin elastic cartilaginous flap, so food does not enter the larynx.

**Airways.** The trachea is a straight tube reaching the mid-thoracic cavity, where it divides at the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra into right and left primary bronchi. These divide repeatedly into secondary and tertiary bronchi and bronchioles, ending in very thin terminal bronchioles. The trachea, bronchi and initial bronchioles are supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings. Each terminal bronchiole gives rise to many thin, irregular-walled, vascularised alveoli; bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli form the lungs.

**Lungs and chest.** Each lung is covered by a double-layered pleura with pleural fluid that reduces friction. The lungs lie in the air-tight thoracic chamber, bounded by the vertebral column dorsally, the sternum ventrally, the ribs laterally and the dome-shaped diaphragm below, so changes in thoracic volume are passed to the lungs.

**Parts.** The conducting part (nostrils to terminal bronchioles) cleans, humidifies and warms air; the exchange part (alveoli and their ducts) is the site of diffusion.

*Diagram:* nostrils, nasal chamber, pharynx, larynx, epiglottis, trachea with rings, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, pleura, diaphragm.

questions.solution_md: Passages, airways, lungs and chest, parts, diagram.

marking_scheme.step: Nostrils to trachea with larynx and epiglottis
Bronchi to alveoli with cartilage rings

questions.stem_md: The owner of a granite-cutting workshop refuses to buy masks for his workers, arguing that “the nose and windpipe already filter out dust, so the lungs are safe”. Evaluate his argument, using what you know about the conducting part of the respiratory system and about occupational respiratory disorders, and recommend what should be done.

answer.model_answer_md:
**What is right in the argument.** The conducting part, from the external nostrils to the terminal bronchioles, does clear inhaled air of foreign particles, and it also humidifies the air and brings it to body temperature. In everyday life this protects the alveoli from most dust.

**Why it fails here.** Stone-grinding and stone-breaking produce so much fine dust that the body’s defence mechanism cannot fully cope with it. Over long exposure dust reaches the lungs and causes inflammation, which leads to fibrosis, a proliferation of fibrous tissue. Fibrosis causes serious lung damage and makes breathing difficult; the damage builds up slowly, so workers may not notice it until it is serious. Such occupational respiratory disorders are well known in these industries.

**Related risks.** Damaged lungs are less able to exchange gases, and irritants can also inflame the bronchi and bronchioles.

**Judgement and recommendation.** The argument is unsound: natural filtering is enough for ordinary air, not for heavy industrial dust. The owner should provide protective masks and insist on their use, and should also reduce dust at its source, for example by wetting the stone while cutting and by ventilating the workshop. Regular health check-ups would detect lung damage early.

questions.solution_md: Conducting part; why it is overwhelmed; fibrosis; masks.

marking_scheme.step: Conducting part does filter ordinary air
Reasoned judgement with masks and other measures

questions.stem_md: A singer takes a deep breath before holding a long note. Which set of events happens in her chest during this inspiration?

options.text_md: The diaphragm and external intercostal muscles relax, and the pressure in the lungs rises above atmospheric pressure.
The diaphragm relaxes while the ribs are lowered, and the pressure in the lungs stays the same.
The diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, and the pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure.
The lungs expand by their own muscles, and the pressure in the chest rises above atmospheric pressure.

questions.solution_md: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostals enlarges the thorax and lungs, lowering the intra-pulmonary pressure below atmospheric so air enters — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Contraction of the external intercostal muscles increases the volume of the thoracic chamber in which axis?

options.text_md: No axis; it decreases the volume

questions.solution_md: The external intercostals lift the ribs and sternum, increasing the volume in the dorso-ventral axis; the diaphragm acts in the antero-posterior axis — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Air flows out of the lungs during normal expiration because

options.text_md: the intra-pulmonary pressure becomes lower than the atmospheric pressure
the diaphragm contracts and pushes the lungs downward
the alveoli actively squeeze out the air with their own muscles
the intra-pulmonary pressure becomes slightly higher than the atmospheric pressure

questions.solution_md: Relaxation of the diaphragm and intercostals reduces the thoracic and pulmonary volume, raising the intra-pulmonary pressure above atmospheric — option (d).

questions.stem_md: How many times a minute does a healthy adult breathe at rest?
questions.solution_md: A healthy human breathes 12–16 times a minute — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The maximum volume of air that a person can breathe out after a forced inspiration is the
questions.solution_md: Vital capacity (ERV + TV + IRV) is the maximum volume breathed in after a forced expiration or out after a forced inspiration — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A doctor records a patient’s breathing with a spirometer, which measures only the air that moves in and out of the mouth. Which value can the spirometer NOT measure directly?
questions.solution_md: Residual volume remains in the lungs even after a forcible expiration, so it never passes through the spirometer; TV, IRV and VC are all breathed in or out — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which two volumes add up to the functional residual capacity?

options.text_md: Expiratory reserve volume and residual volume
Tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume
Tidal volume and expiratory reserve volume
Inspiratory reserve volume and residual volume

questions.solution_md: FRC = ERV + RV, the air left in the lungs after a normal expiration — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Contraction of the diaphragm helps in inspiration.

**Reason (R):** Contraction of the diaphragm decreases the volume of the thoracic chamber.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true, but R is false: the contracting diaphragm increases the thoracic volume in the antero-posterior axis — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The volume of air inspired or expired during a normal respiration, about 500 mL, is called the ______ volume.
questions.solution_md: Tidal volume.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Expiratory capacity is the total volume of air a person can expire after a normal inspiration, and equals tidal volume plus expiratory reserve volume.
questions.solution_md: True: EC = TV + ERV.

questions.stem_md: A spirometer shows that a boy’s tidal volume is 500 mL and his inspiratory reserve volume is 2800 mL. What is his inspiratory capacity in mL?
questions.solution_md: $\text{IC} = \text{TV} + \text{IRV} = 500 + 2800 = 3300$ mL.

questions.stem_md: A swimmer’s readings are tidal volume 500 mL, inspiratory reserve volume 2600 mL and expiratory reserve volume 1000 mL. Calculate her vital capacity in mL.
questions.solution_md: $\text{VC} = \text{ERV} + \text{TV} + \text{IRV} = 1000 + 500 + 2600 = 4100$ mL.

questions.stem_md: A man has a vital capacity of 4200 mL and a residual volume of 1150 mL. What is his total lung capacity in mL?
questions.solution_md: $\text{TLC} = \text{VC} + \text{RV} = 4200 + 1150 = 5350$ mL.

questions.stem_md: While reading quietly, a girl breathes 15 times a minute with a tidal volume of 500 mL. How many mL of air does she breathe in each minute?
questions.solution_md: $500 \times 15 = 7500$ mL per minute, inside the usual 6000–8000 mL.

questions.stem_md: A lung-function report gives total lung capacity 5800 mL, functional residual capacity 2300 mL and tidal volume 500 mL. Find the inspiratory reserve volume in mL.
questions.solution_md: TLC is FRC plus IC, so $\text{IC} = 5800 - 2300 = 3500$ mL. Since IC = TV + IRV, $\text{IRV} = 3500 - 500 = 3000$ mL.

questions.stem_md: Nerve damage leaves a patient’s diaphragm unable to contract. Explain how this affects inspiration and which muscles can still enlarge the chest.

answer.model_answer_md: Normally the **contracting diaphragm** flattens and increases thoracic volume in the **antero-posterior axis**; without it, inspiration is much **weaker**, as the volume and the fall in lung pressure are smaller. The **external intercostal muscles** can still lift the **ribs and sternum**, enlarging the chest in the **dorso-ventral axis**.

questions.solution_md: Loss of antero-posterior enlargement; intercostals still act.

questions.stem_md: Describe the sequence of events during normal, quiet expiration.

answer.model_answer_md: The **diaphragm and the intercostal muscles relax**, so the diaphragm returns to its dome shape and the ribs and sternum return to their normal positions. The **thoracic and pulmonary volumes decrease**, the **intra-pulmonary pressure rises** slightly above atmospheric pressure, and air is **expelled** from the lungs.

questions.solution_md: Relaxation, volume fall, pressure rise, air out.

marking_scheme.step: Muscles relax; diaphragm and sternum return
Volume falls, pressure rises, air out

questions.stem_md: Define inspiratory capacity, functional residual capacity and total lung capacity, writing each as a sum of respiratory volumes.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Inspiratory capacity (IC):** the total volume of air a person can inspire after a normal expiration; **IC = TV + IRV**.

**Functional residual capacity (FRC):** the volume of air that remains in the lungs after a normal expiration; **FRC = ERV + RV**.

**Total lung capacity (TLC):** the total volume of air in the lungs at the end of a forced inspiration; **TLC = RV + ERV + TV + IRV**, or **VC + RV**.

questions.solution_md: Three definitions with sums.

questions.stem_md: Compare inspiration and expiration under three headings: the state of the diaphragm, the change in thoracic volume, and the intra-pulmonary pressure.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Diaphragm:** in inspiration it **contracts** and flattens; in expiration it **relaxes** and returns to its dome shape.

**Thoracic volume:** in inspiration it **increases** (antero-posterior and dorso-ventral axes, with the external intercostals lifting the ribs and sternum); in expiration it **decreases**.

**Intra-pulmonary pressure:** in inspiration it falls **below atmospheric pressure**, so air enters; in expiration it rises **above atmospheric pressure**, so air leaves.

questions.solution_md: Three contrasts.

questions.stem_md: Explain the mechanism of breathing in humans. Describe the roles of the air-tight thoracic chamber, the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles, and how pressure changes move air in and out.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Principle.** Breathing has two stages, inspiration and expiration. Air moves because a pressure gradient is created between the lungs and the atmosphere: inspiration occurs when the intra-pulmonary pressure is less than atmospheric pressure (a negative pressure in the lungs), and expiration when it is higher than atmospheric pressure.

**Air-tight chamber.** The lungs lie in the thoracic chamber, formed by the vertebral column, sternum, ribs and the dome-shaped diaphragm. It is anatomically air-tight, so any change in its volume is reflected in the pulmonary cavity. We cannot change the lung volume directly; we change the volume of the chest instead.

**Inspiration.** The diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing the volume of the thoracic chamber in the antero-posterior axis. The external intercostal muscles contract and lift the ribs and the sternum, increasing the volume in the dorso-ventral axis. The pulmonary volume rises, the intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, and air rushes into the lungs.

**Expiration.** The diaphragm and the intercostal muscles relax, returning the diaphragm and sternum to their normal positions. The thoracic and pulmonary volumes fall, the intra-pulmonary pressure rises slightly above atmospheric pressure, and air is expelled.

**Extra effort.** Additional abdominal muscles can increase the strength of inspiration and expiration. A healthy person breathes 12–16 times a minute, moving about 500 mL of air in each normal breath.

questions.solution_md: Pressure gradient; air-tight chest; inspiration; expiration.

marking_scheme.step: Inspiration: diaphragm and external intercostals, axes

questions.stem_md: Which pair of partial pressures drives carbon dioxide out of the blood arriving at the lungs and into the alveolar air?

options.text_md: pCO₂ 45 mm Hg in the blood and 40 mm Hg in the alveoli
pCO₂ 40 mm Hg in the blood and 45 mm Hg in the alveoli
pCO₂ 0.3 mm Hg in the blood and 40 mm Hg in the alveoli
pCO₂ 95 mm Hg in the blood and 104 mm Hg in the alveoli

questions.solution_md: Deoxygenated blood has pCO₂ 45 and alveoli 40 mm Hg, so carbon dioxide diffuses from blood to alveoli — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is NOT one of the three major layers of the diffusion membrane in the lungs?

options.text_md: The thin squamous epithelium of the alveoli
The endothelium of the alveolar capillaries

questions.solution_md: The diffusion membrane is made of alveolar squamous epithelium, capillary endothelium and the basement substance; the pleura covers the whole lung — option (b).

questions.stem_md: About what percentage of the oxygen carried in blood is dissolved in the plasma?
questions.solution_md: About 97 percent of oxygen is carried by RBCs and the remaining 3 percent is dissolved in plasma — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In which form is the largest share of carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
questions.solution_md: About 70 percent of carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate, 20–25 percent as carbamino-haemoglobin and about 7 percent dissolved — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Blood flows through the capillaries of an active thigh muscle, where pCO₂ is high and pO₂ is low. What happens to carbon dioxide binding with haemoglobin there?

options.text_md: More carbon dioxide binds to haemoglobin as carbamino-haemoglobin.
Carbon dioxide is released from carbamino-haemoglobin.
Haemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly instead.
Bicarbonate is converted back into carbon dioxide.

questions.solution_md: High pCO₂ and low pO₂, as in the tissues, favour binding of carbon dioxide to haemoglobin; release happens in the alveoli — option (a).

questions.stem_md: During a sprint, the leg muscles become warmer and more acidic and produce extra carbon dioxide. What is the effect on the oxyhaemoglobin reaching those muscles?

options.text_md: It holds its oxygen more tightly than at rest.
It gives up more of its oxygen to the muscles.
It changes into carbamino-haemoglobin without losing oxygen.
It is unaffected, because only pO₂ matters.

questions.solution_md: Higher temperature, more H⁺ and high pCO₂ favour dissociation of oxygen from oxyhaemoglobin, releasing more oxygen to the working muscle — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which set of conditions in the alveoli favours the formation of oxyhaemoglobin?

options.text_md: Low pO₂, high pCO₂, more hydrogen ions and higher temperature
High pO₂, high pCO₂, more hydrogen ions and higher temperature
High pO₂, low pCO₂, fewer hydrogen ions and lower temperature
Low pO₂, low pCO₂, fewer hydrogen ions and lower temperature

questions.solution_md: In the alveoli high pO₂, low pCO₂, lesser H⁺ concentration and lower temperature favour oxyhaemoglobin formation — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In an experiment, an inhibitor blocks the enzyme carbonic anhydrase inside red blood cells. Which form of carbon dioxide transport would fall the most?
questions.solution_md: Carbonic anhydrase speeds the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into carbonic acid and then bicarbonate; bicarbonate carries about 70 percent, so it falls most — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The respiratory rhythm centre, primarily responsible for regulating breathing, is located in the
questions.solution_md: The respiratory rhythm centre is in the medulla; the pneumotaxic centre is in the pons — option (d).

questions.stem_md: While holding her breath under water, a swimmer soon feels a strong urge to breathe. Which change is mainly detected to produce this urge?

options.text_md: A fall in oxygen, sensed by the pneumotaxic centre in the pons
A rise in oxygen, sensed by stretch receptors in the alveoli
A rise in carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions, sensed next to the rhythm centre
A fall in body temperature, sensed by the diaphragm muscle

questions.solution_md: The chemosensitive area next to the rhythm centre is highly sensitive to carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions; the role of oxygen in regulation is quite insignificant — option (c).

**Reason (R):** The solubility of carbon dioxide is 20–25 times higher than that of oxygen.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

**Reason (R):** About 70 percent of carbon dioxide is carried in the blood as bicarbonate.

**Assertion (A):** The pneumotaxic centre can alter the rate of breathing.

**Reason (R):** The pneumotaxic centre is located in the medulla.

Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md: Receptors associated with the aortic arch and the ______ artery can recognise changes in carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion concentration.
questions.solution_md: The carotid artery.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A plot of the percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen against pO₂ gives a sigmoid curve.
questions.solution_md: True: this is the oxygen dissociation curve.

questions.stem_md: Under normal conditions every 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL of oxygen to the tissues. How many mL of oxygen are delivered when 6000 mL of blood passes through the tissues?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{6000}{100} \times 5 = 300$ mL of oxygen.

answer.model_answer_md: About **97 percent** of oxygen is carried by **red blood cells**, bound reversibly to **haemoglobin**, a red iron-containing pigment, as **oxyhaemoglobin**; each haemoglobin molecule carries up to **four** oxygen molecules. questions.stem_md: Explain how carbon dioxide produced in the tissues is converted to bicarbonate and released again at the alveoli. Write the reaction and name the enzyme.

answer.model_answer_md:
RBCs contain a high concentration of **carbonic anhydrase** (a little is in plasma), which speeds the reaction both ways:

$$\ce{CO2 + H2O <=> H2CO3 <=> HCO3- + H+}$$

In the **tissues**, pCO₂ is high, so carbon dioxide combines with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into **bicarbonate** and hydrogen ions. At the **alveoli**, pCO₂ is low, so the reaction runs **backwards**: bicarbonate forms carbonic acid, which gives carbon dioxide and water, and the **carbon dioxide is released** into alveolar air.

marking_scheme.step: Forward in tissues, reverse in alveoli

questions.stem_md: What is the oxygen dissociation curve? Using it, explain why haemoglobin loads oxygen in the lungs but unloads it in a contracting muscle.

answer.model_answer_md:
It is the **sigmoid** plot of the **percentage saturation of haemoglobin** with oxygen against **pO₂**.

In the **lungs**, high pO₂, low pCO₂, fewer H⁺ ions and lower temperature place haemoglobin near the top of the curve, so **oxyhaemoglobin forms**.

In a **contracting muscle**, pO₂ is low while pCO₂, H⁺ and temperature are high; saturation drops along the steep part of the curve, so **oxygen dissociates** and is released to the muscle.

questions.stem_md: State the roles of the respiratory rhythm centre, the pneumotaxic centre and the chemosensitive area in regulating breathing.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Respiratory rhythm centre** (medulla): primarily responsible for regulating the rhythm of breathing.

**Pneumotaxic centre** (pons): moderates the rhythm centre; its signal can **reduce the duration of inspiration** and thereby alter the respiratory rate.

**Chemosensitive area** (beside the rhythm centre): highly sensitive to **carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions**; a rise activates it, and it signals the rhythm centre to adjust breathing so these are eliminated.

questions.stem_md: Explain how oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged at the alveoli and the tissues, and how each gas is transported in the blood.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Exchange.** Gases are exchanged by simple diffusion down partial-pressure gradients at the alveoli and at the tissues. Alveolar air has pO₂ 104 and pCO₂ 40 mm Hg; deoxygenated blood arriving has pO₂ 40 and pCO₂ 45, so oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide into the alveoli. Oxygenated blood (pO₂ 95, pCO₂ 40) reaches tissues with pO₂ 40 and pCO₂ 45, so oxygen moves into the tissues and carbon dioxide into the blood. Carbon dioxide is 20–25 times more soluble than oxygen, and the diffusion membrane (alveolar squamous epithelium, basement substance and capillary endothelium) is much less than a millimetre thick, so diffusion is efficient.

**Oxygen transport.** About 97 percent is carried by RBCs as oxyhaemoglobin, each haemoglobin carrying up to four oxygen molecules; 3 percent is dissolved in plasma. High pO₂, low pCO₂, fewer H⁺ ions and lower temperature in the alveoli favour loading; the opposite conditions in the tissues favour unloading, as the sigmoid oxygen dissociation curve shows. Each 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL of oxygen.

**Carbon dioxide transport.** About 20–25 percent travels as carbamino-haemoglobin, 70 percent as bicarbonate and 7 percent dissolved in plasma. Carbonic anhydrase in RBCs converts carbon dioxide and water to carbonic acid and then bicarbonate in the tissues, and reverses the reaction in the alveoli. Each 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of carbon dioxide to the alveoli.

questions.stem_md: Ravi runs up four flights of stairs, and his breathing becomes faster and deeper within seconds. Explain how the neural system brings about this change, naming the centres and sensors involved, and say why a fall in oxygen is not the main trigger.

answer.model_answer_md:
**What changes.** Climbing stairs makes the leg muscles respire faster, so they release more carbon dioxide into the blood, and hydrogen ions rise with it.

**Sensors.** A chemosensitive area situated next to the respiratory rhythm centre is highly sensitive to carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions. When these rise, the area is activated and signals the rhythm centre to make adjustments so that the extra carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions are eliminated. Receptors associated with the aortic arch and the carotid artery also recognise the changes and send signals to the rhythm centre.

**Centres.** The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla is primarily responsible for regulating breathing; it drives the diaphragm and intercostal muscles harder and more often. The pneumotaxic centre in the pons can moderate the rhythm centre: its signal can reduce the duration of inspiration and so alter the respiratory rate, helping Ravi take faster breaths.

**Result.** Breathing becomes faster and deeper, more carbon dioxide is breathed out and more oxygen taken in, until the levels return to normal.

**Why not oxygen.** The role of oxygen in regulating the respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant; breathing is adjusted mainly by carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions.

questions.solution_md: Stimulus; sensors; centres; result; oxygen insignificant.

marking_scheme.step: More carbon dioxide and H⁺ from muscles

Rhythm centre in medulla; pneumotaxic centre in pons
